stem: The stomach enzyme pepsin works best at about pH 2. What happens to pepsin's activity when it enters the small intestine, where the pH is about 8?
options: It increases, because enzymes work faster at higher pH.
It stays the same, because enzymes are not used up.
It drops sharply, as the higher pH alters pepsin's shape.
It changes so that it digests fats instead of proteins.
explanation: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Far from it, the enzyme's shape (and its active site) changes, so the substrate no longer fits and activity drops.
distractors: A: each enzyme has its own optimum; pepsin's is acidic. B: enzymes are reusable, but they can still be inactivated by the wrong pH. D: an enzyme's job is set by its shape; it doesn't switch to a different substrate.

stem: Why should patients take antibiotics exactly as prescribed, rather than skipping doses or stopping on their own?
options: Misuse lets less-susceptible bacteria survive and spread.
The body stores leftover antibiotic for future infections.
Antibiotics also help clear viral infections.
Extra doses help the immune system make antibodies.
explanation: Using antibiotics incorrectly (skipping doses, stopping on one's own, or using them when they aren't needed) gives bacteria that are less affected by the drug a chance to survive and multiply, which contributes to antibiotic resistance. The prescriber sets the dose and length of treatment, so patients should follow it exactly.
distractors: B: the body does not store antibiotics for later. C: antibiotics do not work on viruses. D: antibodies come from the immune system's response to a pathogen, not from antibiotic doses.

stem: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive trait. A carrier mother and an unaffected father have a son. What is the probability that he has hemophilia?
explanation: Sons get their X from the mother and their Y from the father. The mother (XᴴXʰ) passes Xʰ half the time, so each son has a 1/2 chance of hemophilia.
distractors: A: the mother carries the allele, so a son can be affected. B: the chance that any child (son or daughter) is an affected son. D: only half of the mother's X chromosomes carry the allele.

stem: A tall pea plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a short plant (tt). Half of the offspring are short. What is the genotype of the tall parent?
options: Tt
TT
TT; the short offspring came from mutations.
It cannot be determined.
explanation: Short offspring (tt) must get a t from each parent, so the tall parent must carry t: it is Tt. Tt × tt gives half Tt (tall) and half tt (short).
distractors: B: TT × tt would give all tall (Tt) offspring. C: half the offspring being short is far too many to blame on chance mutations. D: the short offspring reveal the hidden allele; this is the purpose of a test cross.

stem: Deleting one nucleotide near the start of a gene usually harms the protein more than substituting one nucleotide. Why?
options: It shifts how every later codon is read.
It changes only the last amino acid.
It changes only the one amino acid at that spot.
It prevents the gene from being copied at all.
explanation: Codons are read three bases at a time. Deleting one base shifts how every later group of three is read (a frameshift), so most amino acids after that point change, and a stop codon often appears early.
distractors: B: the change starts at the deletion, not at the end of the protein. C: that describes a single substitution; a deletion affects every codon after it. D: the gene can still be transcribed; the message is garbled.

stem: The enzyme lactase splits lactose (milk sugar) into glucose and galactose. What type of reaction is this?
options: Hydrolysis
Dehydration synthesis
Denaturation
Neutralization
explanation: Hydrolysis breaks a bond by adding water. Digestion of larger molecules into smaller units, like lactose into two simple sugars, is hydrolysis.
distractors: B: dehydration synthesis is the reverse: it joins units and removes water. C: denaturation changes a protein's shape. D: neutralization is an acid reacting with a base.

stem: Which element is found in all proteins but not in simple sugars such as glucose?
options: Carbon
Hydrogen
Oxygen
Nitrogen
explanation: Every amino acid has an amino group containing nitrogen. Simple sugars such as glucose contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
distractors: A, B and C: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are found in both carbohydrates and proteins.

stem: Which of these diseases are caused by viruses? Select all that apply.
options: Strep throat
Influenza
Tuberculosis
Measles
HIV/AIDS
explanation: Influenza, measles and HIV/AIDS are viral diseases.
distractors: A and C: strep throat and tuberculosis are bacterial infections, which is why they are treated with antibiotics.

stem: An antacid tablet fizzes as it reacts with water. Which conditions would make the reaction finish fastest?
options: A whole tablet in cold water
A whole tablet in warm water
A crushed tablet in cold water
A crushed tablet in warm water
explanation: Crushing increases surface area, so more particles can react at once, and warmer water makes particles move faster and collide harder. Both speed the reaction.
distractors: A: neither change; the slowest. B: warmer water helps, but the whole tablet has less surface area. C: crushing helps, but cold water slows the particles.

stem: Antacid tablets relieve heartburn caused by stomach acid. How do they change the pH in the stomach?
options: They are bases, so they raise the pH toward neutral.
They are bases, so they lower the pH further.
They are acids, so they raise the pH toward neutral.
They add H⁺ ions, so they raise the pH.
explanation: Antacids contain mild bases, such as magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate. They react with stomach acid, removing H⁺ ions, so the pH rises toward neutral. (Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O; calcium carbonate also gives off CO₂.)
distractors: B: removing acid raises the pH; a lower pH means more acid. C: adding acid would worsen heartburn. D: adding H⁺ would lower the pH, not raise it.

stem: Methane burns according to CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. How many molecules of O₂ are needed to burn 5 molecules of CH₄ completely?
explanation: The equation shows 2 O₂ for every 1 CH₄. So 5 CH₄ need 5 × 2 = 10 O₂.
distractors: A: copies the coefficient from the equation. B: assumes a 1:1 ratio. D: counts oxygen atoms (10 × 2) instead of O₂ molecules.

stem: Burning wood gives off heat and light. How is this reaction classified?
options: Endothermic
A physical change
Exothermic
A decomposition reaction
explanation: A reaction that releases energy to its surroundings is exothermic. Burning (combustion) is exothermic.
distractors: A: endothermic reactions absorb energy from their surroundings. B: burning forms new substances (ash, carbon dioxide, water vapor), so it is a chemical change. D: burning combines fuel with oxygen; it is a combustion reaction, not a decomposition.
